newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian firms see no succour in Euroissues.
newsitem.headline: Indian firms see no succour in Euroissues.

text.p: India's largest commercial bank attracted strong commitments at a global share offering on Thursday, but its pricing brought little cheer to other firms planning Euro stock issues, analysts said on Friday.
"It proved there's latent demand for quality Indian paper," said Ramesh Damani, a member-broker at the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). "But the pricing was awful."

State Bank of India's (SBI) issue of global depositary receipts (GDRs) for $400 million, including $50 million greenshoe, drew commitments for nearly $900 million. A greenshoe is an option allowing a company to retain excess subscriptions.
But SBI had to peg the issue size at $369.98 million because foreign holdings in the equity had reached a 20 percent ceiling prescribed by the Indian government.
The issue was priced at $14.15 per GDR in New York on Thursday, which reflected a small premium of 4.8 percent to its underlying stock, its underwriter Lehman Brothers said.
"Premium?" said one dealer at an European broking firm.
"That's plain gibberish."

Analysts said the premium was based on the average closing price of 239 rupees ($6.70) at the BSE and 240.25 rupees at the National Stock Exchange (NSE) on Thursday. Each GDR represents two underlying shares.
Traders said the SBI share had fallen 8.51 percent between September 23 -- when the bank began roadshows -- and October 3 on relentless selling by foreign funds.
"The (GDR) realisation is substantially sub-optimal to expectations," said one strategist at a Hong Kong broking firm. "The premium is only on paper."
The SBI stock tumbled 11 rupees to 228 at the BSE in late afternoon deals on Friday, hit by news that foreign funds will be unable to buy the share because of the 20 percent cap on investments.

The strategist said foreign funds preferred GDRs to their underlying stock because they offered better capital appreciation and lacked the settlement problems that plagued Indian markets. Foreign institutional investors tried to exit SBI in anticipation of the GDRs, he said.
Analysts said international investors had an appetite for quality Indian paper but the kitty was limited.
"There isn't much money with fund managers until fresh allocations are made in January," the strategist at the Hong Kong broking firm said. "It's going to be a rough ride."
Faced with depressed domestic bourses, several Indian companies want to tap the global market with equity offers but analysts say most of them will have to put their plans on hold.
"There's demand provided you have a good story to tell," said the strategist.
The blue-chip SBI was the first Indian bank to hit the GDR market, but in some sectors like automobiles, foreign funds have used up their allocations.
But a big GDR issue by monopoly telcommunications firm Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL), which is yet to be finalised, can hope to sail through.
"There's enough telecom dedicated funds. It should go through," said Ramnath Iyer, strategist at Peregrine Capital. "There's demand for quality stock."
